This article extends non-classical combinatory logic by incorporating a feature reminiscent of dependent types found in constructive type theory.  Specifically, it illustrates how to derive the axiom of equality induction from the rule of equalities elimination in this improved system.  The derivation is significant as the axiom of equality induction is typically regarded as equivalent to the rule of equalities elimination and the principle of recursive definition, with the former being derivable from the latter in most type theories featuring inductive types.  However, in combinatory logic, where the rule of equalities elimination isn't obviously applicable due to the lack of an explicit induction rule, our approach offers a novel path to achieve the same result.  Notably, our method uniquely utilizes an explicit representation for equalities between terms parameterized by equality reflection, allowing for the derivation of equality induction through a form of eta expansion for the equalities elimination rule.

The anomalous Hall and Chern-Simons currents, driven by both non-abelian and abelian external electromagnetic fields, are examined within the framework of the generalized holographic Wilson-Eilenberger model.  Using a five-dimensional duality transformation, the five-dimensional magnetic and electric fields can be perceived as non-abelian and abelian chiral spin and charge currents, respectively. This is achieved by deriving the "Newtonian" or "near-zone" behavior of the gravitational wave multipoles through an expansion in 1/r, within the metric perturbation expansion. We formulate this using the Regge-Teweldemedhin formalism, deriving general expressions for the multipoles that are valid within the gravitational wave zone. By deriving these expressions with a similar level of precision (post-Newtonian order) in both approaches, we can directly compare and contrast the two formalisms. Through this analysis, we find that dynamic spatial components (h0i) of the gravitational wave metric perturbation contribute to the fourth post-Newtonian order in the quadrupolar mode and the third post-Newtonian order in the current mode. Furthermore, we investigate how this level of precision in the dynamic spatial modes affects the accuracy of the radiative modes in the context of numerical relativity simulations.

  can effectively model complex and diverse distributions, making them

a novel approach to 2D indoor localization is proposed, which overcomes the challenges posed by the infinite possibilities of 3D surface positions.  Our method, which is application-specific and focuses on classifying the vertical variation in height profiles relative to a fixed horizontal interval, yields improved results compared to 3D surface sensing methods when sensor noise is controlled.  By leveraging the independence of the height dimension, our algorithm reduces the number of features required and enhances model efficiency by comparing height profiles along the variable x-axis.  Our method was demonstrated on an integrated system consisting of a Raspberry Pi computer and a 3D time-of-flight sensor, with successful evaluations conducted in various indoor settings.  Moreover, our research provides insight into the potential use of horizontal orientation in improving indoor localization techniques.

A rigorous analysis follows, in which the modified Lorentz media model is utilized to describe the time-varying dipole moments, while ensuring compliance with the conservation of energy principle. Following this, a set of equations derived from Lorentz media is compared to a set of analogous Schrödinger-type equations, which is then applied to a two-photon absorption scenario. A scenario is subsequently considered in which active molecules are uniformly distributed in space and initially occupy their lower energy state; the space is subsequently penetrated by an incident plane wave. To address the challenge of creating high-frequency SETs, we devised and executed an approach based on fabricating short-channel tunnel barriers within a double-gate geometry. This involved optimizing the gate capacitances and creating strong gate coupling for robust voltage control of the tunneling energy levels. Specifically, we achieved significant shifts in threshold voltages greater than 20 mV in response to gate voltage changes, clearly indicating single-electron charging effects and the ability to control electron tunneling in both directions. These outcomes demonstrate the potential of this manufacturing process for producing SETs with reliable single-electron charging and strong gate coupling in future applications.

To study the dynamics of innovation, we develop a theoretical framework that captures the behavior of agents within two distinct markets - an upcoming one and an existing one. The success of gradient-based training methods using a mini-batch approach has largely been attributed to their ability to approximate global optimal solutions to non-convex optimization problems.  The success of contrastive learning-based training methods has remained a mystery to the research community.  The learning dynamics of such methods have not been studied extensively, particularly in the context of self-supervised image classification.  In this study, we examined the global optimal solutions to non-convex optimization problems that arise in contrastive learning and discovered that they are essentially determined by the distribution of training data and are nearly indistinguishable from one another in terms of Kullback-Leibler divergence when they enter the region of low error rates.  Notably, this high degree of equivalence holds even though the contrastive learning objective functions are heavily influenced by training data order and are both non-stationary and non-convex.  Our research also reveals surprising similarities between the global optimal solutions of contrastive learning and those of traditional auto-encoders, and we propose that both types of networks learn to model data distributions through their distinct ways of constructing energy functions.

  formula for conductivity in lattices with finite heat transfer.  The connection
  is based on a specific spectral identity for single-particle properties.  The
  formula derived in the work applies to both staggered and regular magnetic
  fields, and its derivation assumes no limitations on the magnetic field strength.
  The derivation involves the partition trick, an infinite sum that determines
  the Hall conductivity.  Inside this sum, occupied states in Landau levels are
  counted based on their energy relative to the Fermi energy, and they respond to
  the magnetic field by rotating between the up and down spin states.  The
  derived formula can also describe the Hall conductance in periodic (without
  magnetic field) systems.  Additionally, for flat Landau levels, the
  conductivity is equal to $e^2/h$ times an integer that represents the number of
  filled Landau levels at zero temperature.  At finite heat transfer, another
  integer is obtained in the same form, but it is no longer the Chern number; it
  is defined as the difference between the highest and lowest filled fractions of
  Landau levels at $T=0$.  The derived formula is derived in a general form that is
  applicable to both ferromagnetic and paramagnetic systems, and accounts for
  both $E$ and $-E$ particle-hole symmetric systems in a unified manner.

sol-gel synthesis technique has gained significant attention due to its simplicity, versatility, and ability to produce high-quality materials with precise control over composition, making it an ideal method for creating complex oxide materials through solution-based processing. In the context of sol-gel synthesis, we present a novel approach based on the thermodynamic analysis of reaction equilibria, allowing for the prediction of product outcomes, yields, and impurity levels.  This method proves to be a valuable tool for optimizing synthesis routes and parameters, with the potential to enhance yields, minimize impurities, and guide the development of new synthesis pathways.  Our model has been successfully applied to examples including metal-organic chemical vapor deposition and has been extended to include alloy synthesis, but can be adapted to any solution-based synthesis method, including spray pyrolysis and chemical replacement.  These applications pave the way for a more rational and efficient integration of sol-gel synthesis with other thin-film deposition techniques.

Specifically, the scalar and tensor modes experience distinct damping due to the friction induced by the M2 tensor field.  This results in the leading-order gravitational waves in scalar-M22 theory behaving similarly to overdamped systems.  However, the tensor mode's response to the friction induced by the M2 tensor field is comparable to that in critical damping.  As the frequency of gravitational waves increases beyond a threshold, it transitions from exhibiting characteristics of an overdamped system to one of an underdamped system.  This transition may be utilized to impose lower bounds on the mass and coupling constants associated with the M2 tensor field, based on the observed features of primordial gravitational waves.  Notably, primordial gravitational waves with long wavelengths can significantly suppress cosmic structure formation.  Nevertheless, constraints derived from cosmic structure formation can further refine the limits that can be placed on the mass and coupling constants associated with the M2 tensor field.  It is worth mentioning that there are regions in the parameter space where the formation of dark matter halos is undisturbed by long-wavelength gravitational waves, and these areas include both the linear and non-linear regimes.

This is because sound-based positioning is less susceptible to external factors and other simultaneous activities, leading to the potential use of this approach for ecological monitoring and enhancing network applications by combining it with other positioning techniques. However, current methods face a significant hurdle in accurately estimating the cross-correlation function (CCF) peak due to noise interference, which can lead to large peak shifts and incorrect target measurements. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel method called Peak Position Estimation (PPE) that makes use of the physical properties of CCF to provide a robust and unbiased peak estimator with consistent performance, regardless of the type of acoustic signal being used. The PPE approach estimates the true peak position by analyzing the decay behavior surrounding the noisy peak, which is supported by theoretical justification and confirmed by experimental results. The outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which yields substantial reductions in positioning errors and provides more accurate ecological and network assessments compared to traditional methods.

the topic of quantum error correction codes capable of detecting and correcting arbitrary single-qubit errors.  Notable examples include stabilizer codes such as the [[7,1,3]] code and non-stabilizer codes like the binary repetition code of length seven. First, we analyze the error correction capabilities of stabilizer codes, using them as an example, the [[7,1,3]] code and three-qubit phase-flip code, by explicitly calculating their performance under various noise models. For instance, certain attention mechanisms calculate output values based on input and network state information that is not directly observable. This unmeasurable data may be crucial, as it could contain crucial information about the sample's label, thus influencing the network's prediction. This effect is known as context contamination. In this research, we propose a method called Reversibility Analysis (RA) to quantify the degree of context contamination in a neural network by examining the irreversibility of its forward transformation. We re-examine the connection between ACs and cuts through the Jahn-Teller model at finite temperatures, focusing on the self-energy at one-loop level. Consequently, when subtracting the zero-temperature component, the finite-temperature branch point should not appear disproportionately. growing complexity and 
  heterogeneity of modern data landscapes often create significant barriers for organizations 
  seeking to fully leverage their extensive data assets.  To overcome this obstacle, a 
  growing number of data fabric architectures have been proposed to unify diverse data 
  sources into streamlined platforms for efficient data management and management.  To 
  accelerate fabric development, data fabric toolkits have been developed to facilitate 
  various data fabric components and services.  To date, no existing work has offered a 
  comprehensive survey of data fabric architectures and their associated toolkits.  In 
  this paper, we present a detailed survey of data fabric architectures and their 
  associated toolkits.  Our survey begins with an in-depth exploration of data fabric 
  components, including data sources, platforms, applications, and management systems, 
  along with their facilitators.  Next, we examine and discuss representative data fabric 
  architectures and their underlying design principles.  Finally, we identify key future 
  research opportunities in data fabric areas.  To support our survey, we also compile a 
  rich dataset of over 100 research articles and more than 300 data fabric toolkits.

OWSA have the potential to deliver extremely high data transfer rates, resulting in substantial energy savings for mobile devices. Nevertheless, the reliance on OWSA on binary optical signals necessitates the development of new charging control algorithms that take both the data transmission and charging processes into account. This work introduces an innovative scheduling framework based on OWSA and task processing that utilizes binary reverse-engineering to develop optimal scheduling solutions. The proposed scheme leverages energy harvesting from available mmWave and OWSA sources to supply the energy needed for mobile devices to process tasks. The energy harvesting framework considers spatially correlated channels, which also data transmission and OWSA sources are dependent on. With the goal of minimizing the number of failed tasks while limiting the number of times the mobile device uses the mmWave source, an optimal solution is developed through a mixed-integer nonlinear programming method. Furthermore, an enhanced version of the algorithm is proposed by orienting the OWSA source to decrease the number of failed tasks and mmWave usages. The simulation results demonstrate that the enhanced algorithm outperforms the original scheme and other baselines.

  interacting with liquid gallium has been investigated for more than three decades. It exhibits many striking phenomena including spontaneous magnetic field generation. Some studies have conveyed the notion that the interaction between interacting carriers and parametric impurities goes against standard conventions, while others have demonstrated that the system can also operate under deterministic principles, determined by the applied electric and magnetic fields. We present a deterministic approach based on the nonlinear sigma model to demonstrate the collective transport of carriers at high mobility in two-dimensional electron gases. By incorporating a deterministic framework, impurity scattering can be seamlessly integrated into the model, which, upon further development with optical activity, yields the Hall-Effect, observable even in highly mobile systems. Ultimately, our model relates the carrier drift velocity to the applied electric field, replicating the Lorentz force outcome in the clean limit and displaying the characteristic parabolic relationship between carrier drift velocity and the square of the applied electric field in the interacting system.

When a small black hole swallows a star it either accretes mass or merges with the larger black hole, thus feeding the system and potentially powering an observable transient.  We investigate how general relativistic effects can influence this process, possibly causing the small black hole to be ejected from the cluster, or trapped within it.  We also examine scenarios where it is released with high velocity, or becomes trapped with short-period, allowing it to devour another star on its own, or even another black hole.  We argue that general relativistic interactions may significantly affect the initial conditions needed for these subsequent events.  We use general relativistic tidal disruption curves as well.  We find that including spin can significantly alter the tidal disruption curve, or even generate long-lived gravitational waves emitters. Although there are no available vaccines or treatments for Dengue fever, urban areas in South America have seen significant outbreaks recently, indicating that existing control measures require improvement or new strategies to be implemented.  This study identifies key parameters that can indicate the spread of Dengue fever in urban areas and proposes two performance metrics to assess the effectiveness of control measures and predict future cases.  Furthermore, it offers optimal values for these parameters based on observed data and evaluates various control strategies, including those used in Mexico City.  According to the results, existing measures may only delay new Dengue fever cases by a few weeks, but they can be significantly reduced with improved vector control, as demonstrated by the performance predictions made in Mexico City. within astrophysical and geophysical fluids, the quasi-geostrophic turbulence (QGT) model offers an effective framework for investigating such processes.  Our research aims to test the consistency of the geostrophic frontogenic theory, which posits that turbulent flows generate fronts through the quasi-linear mechanism's ability to concentrate enstrophy.  This theory suggests the existence of a balance between turbulent dissipation and the formation of fronts, which we investigate by analyzing the ability of enstrophic structures to survive along diagonals in phase space.  Our numerical simulations, run over extended durations, reveal varying levels of concentration in QGT spectra, indicating that the quasi-linear mechanism's effectiveness differs significantly across different regimes. These findings reveal that the phase-space structure and the resulting PDFs are highly dependent on the parameters that define the turbulence, thereby challenging the notion of a universal equilibrium state in QGT.  However, our results do support the geostrophic frontogenic theory, since regimes with diagonal phases and Gaussian distributions indicate that the mean flow variance is larger than the turbulent fluctuation, thus ensuring the stability of turbulent patches.

(UHE) neutrino observations will likely be shaped by upcoming large-scale detectors such as CTA, SWGO, HAWC-II, and others. These new projects will enable more significant studies of UHE neutrino sources and the propagation of the neutrino field. Nevertheless, neglecting the effects of the Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) in these studies remains prevalent. This is because the impact of LIV on the neutrino field depends heavily on the characteristics of the source and the specific properties of the neutrino, including its energy at emission. This, in turn, influences whether the neutrino field can be effectively detected by Earth-based observers. This situation differs from the traditional approach of applying LIV modifications to all possible interactions in the standard model, regardless of the actual neutrino field strength, which could lead to unrealistic conclusions regarding detectability. To address this, we propose modifying the threshold condition to incorporate the fraction of the critical density, denoted as $\eta$, in the LIV parameters. This condition directly impacts the ultimate detection rate of neutrinos, which can then vary significantly based on the properties of various sources, resulting in detection rates that differ by several orders of magnitude and could potentially indicate the direction of future research. This, ultimately, underscores the importance of considering Earth-based and based analyses in the context of LIV.

In this study, we examine this issue more closely, focusing on the spatial and temporal aspects of wave-field variations, and propose a new, physically sound formulation for the FWI gradient that accounts for these aspects. second order linear ODEs in the complex plane has been successfully solved
in previous studies. However, in those solutions, the boundary values of

Unfortunately, these methods' effectiveness is limited due to their reliance on supervised learning and the unavailability of accurately labeled real-world datasets.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have started exploring data-free anti-spoofing techniques that leverage information from legitimate biometric data to create effective detection models.  However, current data-free anti-spoofing techniques have significant limitations, such as the inability to utilize real-world data and the reliance on pre-trained models.  To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel two-stage data-free anti-spoofing framework called Spatial Frequency Domain Disentanglement and Reconstruction.  In the first stage, our approach develops a discriminative disentangler in the spatial frequency domain that separates the authentic information from the fake data.  In the second stage, our method employs an adaptive reconstruction network to reconstruct the spoof data using the separated authentic information and original features, and then compares this reconstruction to the original data for effectiveness.  We evaluated our proposed framework on two public datasets, MAFTA and ORL.  Experimental findings reveal that our approach outperforms existing data-free anti-spoofing techniques across different scenarios.

Squeezed states are a versatile class of nonclassical light with enhanced sensitivity, playing a key role in quantum optics and quantum information. This class includes vacuum and coherent states as well as certain V-state examples, but most V-states cannot be produced through standard photon subtraction or amplification from specific input states using a single-mode linear device. This study identifies two-generation circuits consisting of linear devices, photon subtraction/addition, and squeezing operations that can generate single-mode N-squeezed states from the vacuum state for any positive integer N, including previously unreported states. These single-mode N-squeezed states can be factorized as H(n')a†n'V(n) for various H, V, and n', demonstrating their unique characteristics. This research provides practical guidance for producing single-mode nonclassical light with desirable properties, including nonclassicality, high photon numbers, and squeezed components, which is essential for numerous applications in the field.

To overcome this limitation, we propose a mechanism for scalar particle production that bypasses the symmetry constraint, which could lead to the emission of scalar radiation even when the global $U(1)$ charge is zero.  Specifically, by introducing an interaction between the complex scalar particle and a gravitationally uncharged, charged black hole, we demonstrate that if the global $U(1)$ charge of the scalar particle is much smaller than its electric charge, there will be an evaporation process similar to Hawking radiation.  However, if the global $U(1)$ charge is not significantly smaller than the electric charge, the charged black hole first evaporates as a charged object and then, in later stages, it emits a scalar charge and transitions to a neutral, hairy state.  The formation of this scalar hair has observational implications for future gravitational wave detectors, which will be able to distinguish between neutral charged black holes and their scalar hair due to differences in how they ring down.

A key problem in the computation of convolution is that a three-dimensional array must be multiplied by a two-dimensional matrix at each spatial location.  We propose a novel calculation technique for convolution that can be computed using a simple one-dimensional operation at each location in the spatial dimensions.  This new method reduces the memory requirements for convolution layers to match those of a one-dimensional embedding, enabling a fully distributed implementation. Our approach involves solving the conformal decomposition equations in an iterative manner, with a focus on gauge-driven methods where we solve the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints within a 1+2+2 decomposition framework.  By solving these equations iteratively, we can generate data that represents two Schwarzschild black holes moving along the $z$-axis.  This process includes distributing mass density in spherical patterns, choosing the trace of the extrinsic curvature based on an approximate equation, and determining the vector field component via an elliptic equation.  Our main equation for this step involves solving the Einstein constraints in an iterative manner, with different implementations of this scheme yielding comparable results.  We also explore alternative methods for determining the curvature in this context, along with numerical solutions for these equations using finite elliptical methods and multigrid techniques.  Ultimately, this study can be viewed as both a technical exploration and an educational overview of constructing initial data in the context of general relativity.

Previously made assumptions about quantum systems have been criticized for not being consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics.  This work takes a different approach, deriving the general mathematical framework that defines a quantum experiment based on the basic principles of quantum mechanics, without needing any additional assumptions.  This framework enables the calculation of information gained from any physical experiment, whether involving measurements from classical detectors or more complex scenarios with multiple outcomes, all the way to experiments performed by EPR detectors. To investigate this intricate relationship between the components enabling personalized computing and those hindering its safe release, our paper introduces an extended version of the Technology Acceptance Model, incorporating the concepts of privacy and security. field theories in spatially curved settings, focusing on the behavior after curvature scale, for fields that are not tightly bound. The Heisenberg dynamics yield a complex evolution operator in curvature space, resulting in the vacuum state's point spread in field and momentum. The spread rates are determined by the curvature scale and the field's equation of state in flat space. Once past this scale, momentum is effectively measured, while the field remains in a quasi-isotropic and time-dependent state. The theory obeys laws of isotropy, allowing for an approximation of field expectation values and momentum spread. The momentum rate of change is set by the adiabatic invariant of a 3D quantum harmonic oscillator. The field operator can be expressed in terms of two annihilation operators with frequency set by the momentum rate of change, and it transforms as a conformal scalar under time dilation. This allows for a natural vacuum state in de Sitter space, and correlations are influenced by flat-space scattering lengths and by the ratio of Planck's constant to curvature scale. The results hold for all quadratic Hamiltonians and demonstrate that quantum entanglement arises from scattering and that both real and momentum spaces are fundamental to cosmology's quantum dynamics.

of overcoming certain fundamental constraints in information theory.  To support this claim, we develop a demon capable of transcending the conventional Szilard's cycle and Landauer's principle.  However, we show that this success comes with a corresponding increase in the mutual information between the demon and the system, which in turn can be interpreted as a tax paid for the demon's gains.  This result implies that the total change in information - system, demon and their interaction - is non-negative, and that no free lunch can be achieved in information.  We further explore the relationship between the demon and the erasure cost, and it is found that the demon's operations can be seen as a trade-off between reducing the demon's stored information and increasing the mutual information between the demon and the system.  This relationship shows that an erasure operation cannot reduce the demon's information more than the desired decrease in mutual information, and any attempt to do so will result in an excessive cost.  We support our findings with illustrative examples and robustness checks.  Our model is robust to variations in the process of erasing the demon, and in the dynamics of both the demon and the system, and can be implemented using different types of physical models, including quantum systems.

Object detection algorithms address this issue by generating bounding box coordinates.  These coordinates serve as input to detection heads, which generate recognition outputs. Imperfect coordinates result in inclusion of irrelevant background and exclusion of parts of the object, hindering effective object identification.  Building on this understanding, we introduce the LowQual-RF concept, an idea of using low-quality images to generate visual representations centered on the object of interest (see Fig.1). We integrate the QRF into the popular two-stage detector Faster R-CNN to produce the Framework called FASER. algorithms exist for a single type of atomic operation across different memory consistency models, very few can achieve simultaneous use for multiple atomic operations. Researchers are on the path of developing concurrent algorithms that can be applied across various memory consistency models for weak atomic operations, which would yield significant benefits such as more efficient shared memory systems and simpler concurrent program developments. This paper introduces two concurrent algorithms for the read-modify-write (RMW) operations that can be executed on a weak atomic bit, specifically a SWAB.  The first algorithm, a three-collision RMW algorithm based on compare-and-swap (CAS), and the second, a two-collision algorithm using a stronger RMW operation of a double-sized word, are both capable of emulating an infinite number of infinite-sized compare-and-swap operations on a single-bit compare-and-swap machine. Notably, the proposed algorithms are the initial ones to utilize a weak atomic operation of an infinite number of bits in a SWAB machine for compare-and-swap and read-modify-write tasks, respectively, as demonstrated through the infallibility theorem. Both algorithms are also verifiable through coq, which should serve as a starting point for developing more sophisticated data structures and concurrent systems.

rising numbers of mobile devices and a growing dependence on mobile connectivity.  To meet future demands, 6G networks must be designed with AI-powered control planes that can dynamically allocate resources in real-time.  To speed up complex optimization problems in resource management, researchers have developed cutting-edge cutting-stock techniques inspired by retail applications.  Unfortunately, these approaches depend on precise data which is often difficult to obtain in network settings.  To overcome this challenge, we propose a flexible framework for wireless traffic management that combines hard constraints with deep learning-based estimation and optimal substructure exploitation.  This framework allows us to determine the minimum hardware requirements, including the number of necessary access points and widths of wireless channels under various constraints.  Our approach consists of two stages: 1) a real-time stage for allocating resources within the limited hardware available, and 2) a planning stage for determining the optimal hardware requirements to satisfy predicted traffic requirements.  In both stages, we develop novel methods to tackle the complex problem of optimal resource allocation by combining the best-known lower bounds with upper bounds derived from the best feasible solutions found so far.  Our simulations show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of throughput, channel utilization, and minimization of hardware requirements, with only a negligible increase in computational overhead.

to address the severe performance decrease of self-supervised learning (SSL) models when they suffer from label corruption misclassification. These models leverage user feedback to adjust the bounding boxes that enclose the mislabeled images. Yet, traditional user-centered approaches rely on hand-crafted rules which require prior knowledge and do not adapt well to diverse, complex, and varied noise patterns. In this study, we introduce a novel approach named U^2 learning, an unsupervised and universal framework that optimizes this process. U^2 learning starts by using the original corrupted labels as rough starting points for the object within the label bounding box. It then utilizes visual similarity to refine the outer boundaries of the label bounding box and achieves improved results. As a result, U^2 learning enhances the performance of SSL models without needing user-rule knowledge and outperforms other methods in terms of efficiency on both synthetic and real-world noise patterns. Moreover, since U^2 learning is an unsupervised and universal approach, it can be applied seamlessly to any existing SSL framework.

simple to complex biological systems, can be effectively modeled using differential equations. By analyzing the orbits and fixed points within these models, researchers gain insights into the long-term behavior of populations described by these equations. The Jacobian matrix plays a crucial role in determining the stability of critical points and determining the form of local orbits around these points. However, the Jacobian matrix's limitations in capturing the complexity of global orbits in ecosystems have prompted scientists to explore alternative methods. Recent studies have demonstrated that Jacobian matrices derived from polynomial vector fields may have infinite positive zeros for all eigenvalues, thereby restricting their ability to describe global orbits. Building on this knowledge, our research extends the application of Jacobian matrices to the domain of cell cycle regulatory networks, utilizing a system of ordinary differential equations based on Jacobi networks to model biological regulation.  Although previous investigations into network topology have highlighted the absence of stable limit cycles in these types of networks, our study focuses on examining the conditions under which these fixed points achieve asymptotic stability, especially when assuming that gene transcription and translation processes occur instantly. By applying the Jacobian matrix analysis to nodes that do not directly regulate each other, we derive novel, data-driven, and biologically interpretable sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability, thereby overcoming recent theoretical limitations.

in transformation-based models (TMs) impact their performance, efficiency, and ability to generalize.  TMs are efficient, data-efficient language understanding systems that learn through a minimal number of examples by acquiring a vector-based mapping from input to output.  Our analysis covers the common projection layer and a novel coefficient-based alternative that requires significantly fewer parameters and computational resources. , first proposed in 1994, describes the movement of a warp drive through spacetime. It was initially intended to investigate whether an object could travel faster than the speed of light, but at the time it was put forward, the concept of an Alcubierre wave could not be fully understood due to limitations in computing power. Today, with advances in supercomputing, complex numerical simulations can be run on the Schrödinger and Dirac equations using the Alcubierre metric, enabling researchers to explore how the metric influences large-scale structures and even small particles. However, these simulations have also revealed that the Alcubierre drive creates significant problems, including the distortion of any nearby matter, radiation that could be deadly to living organisms, and the trapping of particles within it.

monoxide molecules in the
  outermost layers of the white dwarf HD 40135, which was previously
  studied by \citet{Kilic11}.  \citet{Kilic11} found no silicon
  monoxide molecules around this star.  However, later observations
  discovered the presence of silicon dioxide molecules around HD 40135
  \citep{Tu13}.  The newly discovered carbon monoxide molecules pose a

  abundant molecule in the star's atmosphere.  Yet carbon monoxide has been

  molecules.  This phenomenon cannot be explained by current dust formation

  dioxide or the invalidation of underlying assumptions in the dust
  formation theory for this specific case of the HD 40135 star.

gained significant popularity in the field of pattern recognition due to its unique feature of generating an interpretable inverse function.  This capability allows for pinpointing specific input components that directly influence a model's prediction output.  However, the development of implicit models has been heavily focused on image-based applications, resulting in limitations when it comes to handling high-dimensional data such as text.  To address this limitation, we present a new class of implicit neural networks named Quadratic Neural Networks (QNN).  These networks are capable of effectively processing text data while maintaining the ability to interact with higher-dimensional inputs, all achieved through employing quadratic neurons.  These neurons are designed to process higher-order inputs and generate target outputs through precise and interpretable operations.  As a result, we are able to identify specific words that have a significant impact on model predictions in both straightforward and nuanced ways.  Our research demonstrates that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to current state-of-the-art models while offering the distinct advantage of interpretability.

  developing forward models that can be paired with learning-based approaches.
  This partnership allows the use of partial differential equation (PDE)-constrained
  neural network methods to tackle reconstruction problems.  Unfortunately, the
  accuracy of these approaches relies heavily on utilizing precise forward models.
  However, obtaining such accurate models can be impractical in certain cases. As
  an alternative, this paper explores the potential of employing data-driven
  surrogate models for the forward operator.  These models are trained to
  approximate the forward operator based on numerically simulated or experimentally
  acquired data.  Although this approach has shown some success, there remains a
  lack of understanding on when these learning-based solutions yield accurate

of distributed stochastic gradient descent.  By analyzing various forms of this algorithm, this paper distinguishes between communication costs (sending data to neighbors and/or coordinator) and coordination costs (waiting for neighbors and/or coordinator).  Specifically, this paper separates communication costs into sending a whole batch or individual gradient samples and coordination costs into sending whole batches or individual gradient samples.  This distinction is significant as it highlights the trade-offs between communication and coordination.  In contrast, most existing research conflates communication and coordination costs.  This distinction allows for a clearer examination of the effects of neighborability and update rules on coordination.  Our analysis encompasses four update rules: i.i.d., square mile, bounded, and bounded square mile.  Our findings reveal that the choice of square mile vs. i.i.d. has a minimal effect on coordination.  Nevertheless, the find best performer may vary based on coordination costs and batch size.  This research offers the most in-depth analysis to date of the trade-offs between communication and coordination.  It clearly demonstrates the importance of considering both coordination and communication in evaluating the efficiency of distributed optimization algorithms.

common metaphor in over 300 languages globally, but the phrase "Like day and night" is far less frequently encountered, despite conveying a similar meaning. This phenomenon may be attributed to sequential effects, which suggest that the order of elements in a comparison is not arbitrary and is influenced by inherent characteristics of those elements. According to Chafe's (1994) Ocuense Hierarchy, elements positioned further along the spectrum of animacy, humanness, and so on, are more likely to be used in comparisons, which seems to align with the observed frequency disparity. However, an examination of the English words 'day' and 'night' does not entirely support this theory. Although both terms refer to periods of time, 'day' is often associated with activity and movement, while 'night' is linked to stillness and the absence of light, as described by the dynamicity hypothesis. This study aims to validate the dynamicity hypothesis by incorporating both cross-linguistic data from multiple English dialects and non-English languages, as well as child language acquisition evidence. Our analysis suggests that cross-linguistic patterns do support the dynamicity hypothesis, while the Ocuense Hierarchy fails to account for the observed frequency disparities in a significant number of languages.

has been recently introduced as a tool to
  identify the origin of species that have undergone hybridization and self-crossing.
  Given genomic data from several present-day species, a persistent phylogeny can
  be viewed as a way of constructing a filtered version of genomic data which
  helps in constructing a present-day phylogeny that is consistent with the
  processed data and maintains statistical significance.
  In this work, we address two key concerns related to present-day phylogenies:
  detecting inconsistencies due to noise or data loss, creating a reliable
  present-day phylogeny that reflects both biological and statistical validity.
  To accomplish this, we develop a robust present-day phylogeny framework based
  on a rigorous statistical model, considering all possible filtered versions of
  genomic data.
  This framework utilizes a statistical model to identify the most favorable
  persistent phylogeny among those that are consistent with the processed data.
  To explore the broader scientific community's perspective on reliable
  present-day phylogenies, we conducted a series of experiments through surveys,
  leading to the following findings:
  (1) researchers face challenges in detecting inconsistencies in their data,
  (2) constructing a robust present-day phylogeny requires combining noise
  detection and handling missing data.

Studies have shown that multiple viral proteins work in concert to facilitate this process, but the precise nature of these interactions is not fully understood. To address this knowledge gap, we employed the technique of co-evolution analysis to identify potential partners for each SARS-CoV-2 entry protein. Using advanced bioinformatics tools, we screened for structural and functional compatibility among predicted partners, ultimately producing a detailed map of interdependent proteins that could work together to enable virus entry. When tested in silico, mutating these identified proteins would need to occur simultaneously to have any effect on the infection process. Next, we analyzed existing experimental data to confirm the functionality of several proposed protein-protein interactions and found evidence supporting the joint contribution of these proteins to the infection process. Building on this information, we developed a metabolic model of the SARS-CoV-2 entry process that relies on the coordinated function of these interdependent proteins, which in turn affected predictions of protein essentiality. Overall, our study highlights the significant contributions of bioinformatics to virology and provides a framework for identifying complex, multi-protein systems that enable virus entry.

concepts related to manifolds with a symplectization structure: stable contact homology and a novel type of Hamiltonian path, called symplectizable Hamiltonian path.  Our main result shows that the condition for a link to be a contact boundary on a non-degenerate, compact manifold with a symplectization structure can be characterized by an infinite series of counting intersection points between transversal transversal sections, which are themselves linked via a symplectizable Hamiltonian path.  Our framework is particularly flexible and allows for the construction of numerous symplectization structures with diverse properties, including the ability to alter the diffeomorphism type of the interior of a handlebody while keeping the boundary fixed.  In addition, we demonstrate that the condition for a link to be a contact boundary on a compact manifold is closely connected to the count of contact homology cycles.  This connection becomes especially useful when considering a link component that does not satisfy the condition for a contact boundary, while other components do form the boundary of the link.  As a result, we can recover a relationship similar to the one found by Hendricks and Scaduto on Heegaard Floer homology.

research focus on identifying signatures of life in spectral data from distant planets. For this purpose, a new method has been developed to simulate these spectra accurately. This method, based on a refined quantum model of atmospheric molecules, significantly reduces the computational cost while maintaining high levels of precision. In contrast to previous methods that utilized stochastic sampling, this new approach determines which frequencies to keep directly, leveraging sparse computation to target the most impactful regions of the spectrum. We demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to several key molecules often found in exoplanet atmospheres, including $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{HCl}$ and $NH_2OH$, and successfully reproduce their experimental cross-sections and scattering phases within acceptable margins of error. The efficiency and scalability of the algorithm are showcased through computations on both single processors and high-performance computer systems, and the code is made openly available for others to use.

learning has sparked significant interest in the potential of lighter models that perform tasks quicker and use computational resources more effectively.  However, in applications where models are deployed on edge devices, especially in computer vision, maintaining high accuracy while reducing model size can be quite challenging.  This difficulty stems from computers typically using 2D images, which often require a substantial increase in input data for accurate classification, leading to a higher computational expense.  Moreover, unlike NLP, there isn't an abundant supply of labeled data available for training these lighter models.  This research introduces a novel approach, known as Sparse Connection Sharing (SCS), that reduces the number of parameters in a neural network while preserving performance by grouping and reusing activation patterns.  The SCS model exhibits 2x faster inference times, achieves similar accuracy to conventional networks of the same architecture, and excels in low-data classification.  Additionally, this model can be trained using far fewer computational resources, making it an ideal solution for computer vision tasks on edge devices.

has become an integral part of the clinical workflow in healthcare facilities worldwide, with significant investments made by healthcare payers.  Despite these investments, many users are not fully utilizing the EHR system, an issue referred to as the "last mile problem."  To address this challenge, our study investigates the impact of advanced clinical decision-making features integrated into the EHR interface.  Through the development of three distinct prototypes with progressively enhanced features, including automatic diagnosis suggestions, risk assessments, and personalized clinical guidelines, we conducted a controlled experiment involving 40 clinicians who interacted with the prototypes and completed a series of clinical tasks while being recorded and evaluated through think-aloud protocols.  Statistical analyses revealed that the inclusion of these decision-making features had a minimal negative effect on the EHR users' performance, an interesting finding that runs counter to common assumptions and has the potential to reshape our understanding of the clinical decision-making process and the design of modern EHR systems.

classical Hubble bubble dynamics in an de Sitter universe.  The probability of tunneling into a universe with lower vacuum energy is increased by quantum gravity, causing the multiverse to reach an equilibrium of bubble collisions.  The quantum gravitational correction is calculated by modifying the de Sitter action with a potential $r^2$-squared term, thereby enabling the analysis of the effect using a Schrodinger equation for the universe wave function.  The de Sitter universe evolution is found to be analogous to an inverted oscillator, leading to the calculation of quantum gravitational corrections to the flux emitted from the bubble using an analogy to the universe occupying a coherent state in an ordinary harmonic oscillator.  The universality of the de Sitter solution is exploited to apply this calculation to various quantum gravity theories that stabilize the cosmological constant, including $R^2$ gravity.  The result for the flux of bubbles tunneling into a universe with lower vacuum energy in $R^2$ gravity is related to the universal $r_2$-squared coefficient in the quantum gravitational expansion of the de Sitter wave function.  This coefficient is derived from the one-loop effective action for a scalar field in de Sitter space.  The result for the flux in $R^2$ gravity is found to be proportional to the field's zero mode expectation value squared in the de Sitter universe.

Furthermore, our approach is robust to reflections and  ambient light interference which are common light-source  interference problems with ToF sensors. Through a series of  comprehensive experiments using both synthetic and real  datasets, our framework demonstrates the framework's ability  to outperform existing tracking approaches in various scenarios.

Despite its value, studying this process is complicated as the possible edges to consider change as the process progresses, making it less like a true random graph model and more like a conditional procedure. This study introduces an analytical tool for addressing this conditionality in a specific subclass of graphs that follow this procedure. This subclass can be characterized by replacing the procedural aspect of the graph's construction with a set of independent, but potentially dependent, events. This analytical tool is then applied to determine specific threshold properties of connected components and connectivity within the process. This new regime has been demonstrated in various experimental setups, including trapped ions and superconducting quantum circuits, but its theoretical underpinnings remain largely unexplored.  To address this knowledge gap, we developed a method to derive the Gibbs state for classical stochastic systems and applied it to solve master's equation problems for two-level quantum systems.  Specifically, we investigated the structure of the drive-corrected diagonal elements in the steady state near equilibrium and found that their amplitudes can be expressed as classical probabilities associated with the Hamiltonian's energy levels in the absence of driving forces.  These findings also reveal that the energy level spacings of two-level systems under driving forces exhibit similar classical dynamics.  Our research also reveals that the quantum Zeno effect and resonant two-level systems both map onto their classical counterparts.  Notably, the amplitude of the quantum Zeno effect's classical analogy is determined by the ratio of the system's decoherence and driving frequencies.  As a result, our findings hold significant implications for the design of control pulses in quantum information processing.

, informal summary of key concepts, issues, and findings in the study of random matrices. 
  It covers background information on basic matrix properties, provides an overview of random matrix applications, explains fundamental facts from this field, and discusses some current areas for further research.

A growing body of evidence suggests that models trained on large, annotated datasets are influenced by the spatial arrangement of objects within the training data, a phenomenon known as location bias. This occurs when models develop an excessive dependence on specific image features that coincide with object locations and are correlated with their semantic content. A model exhibiting location bias will classify objects correctly during initial testing but fails when objects are moved to a new location associated with a different class through data shift. A position-aware bias measurement that quantifies this issue and a bias-reduction strategy that assigns lower weights to highly correlated locations are proposed to mitigate its effects. Our research demonstrates the existence of location bias in models trained using models trained on large, annotated models and demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method in mitigating its effects.

plet containing volatile and non-volatile solutes is influenced by the presence of solutes in multiple ways.  The accumulation of solutes at the droplet base creates a concentration gradient that hinders further evaporation, which can be controlled or amplified through the introduction of solutes with specific transport properties.  The deformation of the droplet shape due to internal flow and the resulting shape changes also play a significant role.  We developed a comprehensive theoretical framework, based on variational principles, to model the evolution of droplet shape, taking into account the effects of solute accumulation.  This approach is applicable to droplets with any base shape and results in predictive insights regarding the deformation of droplets.  We also explored the impact of solute transport properties on the shape of droplets during evaporation.  In particular, we discovered that slowly diffusing solutes produce circular-shaped droplets with rapid evaporation rates due to the development of an impenable solid layer, whereas other solute profiles result in an oscillating deformation of the droplet and complex internal flow patterns that may influence solute deposition.  We demonstrated the efficacy of our theoretical model in reproducing the dynamics of droplet formation. This paper introduces a robust visual-inertial odometry method for UAVs affected by wind-induced disturbances and sudden gusts.  Our proposed system, integrating visual and inertial data, ensures safe navigation and maneuvering of UAVs in unpredictable wind conditions.  To enhance the reliability of state estimations, we develop a stereo visual odometry algorithm resistant to wind-induced impacts.  This system achieves precise relative poses between frames with minimal drift.  However, UAV visual features can be dislodged or obscured due to wind forces, resulting in unreliable state estimates. When the gravity decreases rapidly with radius, the extremal distance behaves similarly to what is observed in black holes for ultra-spinning Kerr singular rings.  However, a gradual decrease in gravity allows the extremal distance to become infinitely large, even in rapidly spinning objects. Gravitational waves and thermal radiation from accretion disks also reflect the extremal distance, utilizing the spin parameter as their source of information. The extremal distance in rapidly spinning KERR black holes can be nearly infinitely large, whereas the extremal distance in compact objects with gravity that decreases rapidly with radius will always remain finite.

findings highlight the importance of incorporating uncertainty handling into both
processing and analysis when applying machine learning techniques to the

  currently rely on piecewise linear approximations of the neural network
  function. The problem of computing the exact minimum value of a neural
  network over a non-trivial input polytope is an NP-hard challenge. An
  ideal algorithm for this task would be capable of identifying specific
  suboptimal solutions within a predetermined number of steps. No such
  exact methods are known that achieve this for neural networks with more
  than a few layers. We propose utilizing stochastic sampling of the
  input features in neural networks to obtain globally optimal certification
  results in polynomial time. This sampling strategy allows us to probe
  different parts of the neural network by randomizing the linear layers
  associated with each neural network layer, thereby obtaining multiple
  valued outputs for a single neural network. We show that this process can
  be modelled as a factor analysis problem, in which we can apply statistical
  tools to find locally optimal solutions and use them to update the neural
  network. We experiment with this algorithm on various neural network
  architectures and certify at least 27% more input polytope volumes for
  ReLU networks compared to the state of the art. Our method can also
  efficiently certify high-volume boxes for networks with more than 10
  hidden layers.

This is because the common practice of assessing a model on the held-out portion of training data can lead to significant inaccuracies, especially when the amount of data used for evaluation is limited.  This issue is compounded by the typical evaluation procedure of resetting and independently training the model before testing, which results in two distinct models being compared.  We investigate these complications in detail and propose a unified evaluation framework that incorporates the effects of model optimization and incorporates a verification component to validate implicit assumptions made in standard assessment methods.  Our research indicates that evaluation metrics calculated from training held-out sets are unreliable and do not accurately reflect the model's true performance.  Moreover, we discover that the model architecture and loss function play more significant roles in evaluation results than does the amount of training data.  Finally, our work unveils new, counterintuitive findings about the influence of optimization on evaluation results, revealing a non-monotonic relationship between data amount and performance, as well as a superior evaluation result when evaluating less performant models with larger datasets.  Our work serves to draw the attention of the recommender community to the practical challenges involved in assessing these systems and underscores the importance of developing robust evaluation methods.

a Torenzan cycle of length k in a graph G can be calculated efficiently, provided that the degree of vertices in G is limited to at most 3.  However, determining the existence of Torenzan cycles in graphs with higher-degree vertices is not fully understood.  This project aims to enhance the existing algorithms for detecting Torenzan cycles in graphs with higher-degree vertices.  Our algorithm can calculate the number of Torenzan cycles in a graph with n vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$, where each instance is completed within time $O(n^{\floor*{\frac{\Delta-1}{2}}+1})$.  This represents an improvement of 0.5 in the degree parameter compared to the previous bound of $\floor*{\frac{\Delta}{2}}+1$ by Grochow and Saxton.  We also provide an alternative calculation method for a smaller bound of Torenzan cycles in graphs with odd $\Delta$, specifically $\floor*{\frac{\Delta-2.5}{2}}+1= \floor*{\frac{\Delta-1}{2}}+1$, though this bound is not meaningful when considering integer values of $\Delta$.

Our investigation into the underlying factors contributing to the elevated performance of RRM takes relative entropy minimization (REM) as a point of comparison.  Concretely, we develop a theoretical link between RRM and REM, and our analysis reveals that the primary distinction between the two methods revolves around the degree to which each prioritizes resolving difficult classification instances.  Moreover, we establish a direct connection between the method's generalization capabilities and the distribution of classification instances it addresses.  In particular, RRM's relative entropy can be decomposed into two components, one of which quantifies the method's difficulty focus in terms of class imbalance and can explain RRM's enhanced performance.  Further, we design and implement Risk Sensitivity Balance (RSB), a novel risk minimization method built on RRM, and our findings from theoretical analysis and experiments confirm that RSB's improved performance over RRM is a direct consequence of RRM and RSBE's difficulty focus. approach to the 2D inverse Compton scattering process, which can occur when relativistic electrons interact with a photon layer in the radiation energy budget of gamma-ray bursts.  this approach scales poorly in larger decentralized settings as it requires 
 information from every agent. To tackle this problem, we introduce DecoTrain, 
 a modified decentralized training framework that reduces sample inefficiency 
 in decentralized environments. DecoTrain enhances sample collection by 
 artificially creating virtual training environments, where trained agents are 
 pitted against one another to generate data. These artificial environments 
 are then replaced with a single real one. DecoTrain also incorporates value 
 function regularization to prevent overfitting of the policy. We evaluated 
 DecoTrain on multiple classic learning problems and found that it yields 
 more robust policies in real-world applications. We also showed that DecoTrain 
 consumes less memory and time than standard decentralized training methods.

By examining the preferred ensemble of configurations for each polymer type in a given incompatible solvent, we can determine the essential features of the system, which can then be used to train machine learning models. These models successfully predict how the required space for polymer ensembles scales with the number of monomers in various combinations of polymers and solvents, even those not previously seen. At the core of this phenomenon is the need to minimize information surprise, which can be greatly influenced by the relative sizes of different monomers. This provides new insights into complex mixtures and alloys of polymers and solidifications of single polymers or solvents that were not considered important before.

  one-dimensional disordered systems, now referred to as "supersolids" and "random
  multiplet" phases.  However, extending this knowledge to one higher dimension poses
  significant challenges, as true glass phases only appear in dimensions of 2 or greater.  In
  this study, we utilize a quantum Ising model to investigate the behavior of
  square-lattice arrays and utilize two different methods to characterize glass
  transitions: computational gauge-trotter evolution and statistical replica
  ansatz.  By combining these approaches, we are able to effectively identify glass
  transitions in systems of up to 16 sites without relying on difficult to obtain
  large-system data.  Our experiment shows that the glass transition in these smaller
  systems occurs at a very accessible level of disorder, and may even be observable
  using current quantum simulators, and and we are able to find that the transition
  level is around 2.4 for systems of 8 or more sites.

We develop a numerical framework to investigate the impact of black hole precession on gravitational wave forms, using the General Relativistic two-body simulation method.  By isolating precession effects through nearly equal-mass and mass-asymmetric binaries, we identify key precession-driven modes in waveforms.  We also identify how the neutron star debris interacts with the larger black hole, leading to a jet-like motion.  We identify how the precessing neutron star's spin axis influences the formation of a disk around the black hole.  We demonstrate how our simulation results can be used in future observations of gravitational waves.

often used in visual effects and gaming, can create intricate shadow patterns on bright surfaces. These shadow patterns arise from the interaction of luminous areas and obstructed light, blending dark and light regions with sharp transitions. Traditional display techniques, such as point-based rendering, miss these details because they only render visible high-light areas. In contrast, new display methods using pixel buffers allow for the visualization of these details by sampling the environment map from multiple viewpoints, resulting in a image that conveys depth through shadow details. However, these methods demand significant computational resources and storage. A point-based approach is presented here that balances performance and quality, optimizing the visualization of these intricate shadow patterns on HDR environment maps.
